## Report as received

<!-- Section 1: checked (see Quote check below) -->

1. Cellular and Molecular Pathology of Idiopathic Guttate Hypomelanosis (IGH)

The cellular and molecular literature on idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis (IGH) is modest compared with autoimmune depigmentation disorders such as vitiligo, and several mechanistic questions remain unresolved. Across immunohistochemical, ultrastructural, and translational biopsy studies, findings separate into directly observed features versus proposed mechanisms.

Established Findings (Direct Observations in Human IGH Lesions)

⚬ Melanocyte number and morphology (reduced, rarely completely absent): Histochemical, immunohistochemical, and ultrastructural biopsies of IGH lesions consistently demonstrate reduced numbers of epidermal melanocytes and decreased epidermal melanin compared with adjacent normal skin, rather than uniform total melanocyte obliteration. In a clinical and histopathological survey of IGH patients, Kim, S. K. et al. (2010; PMID: 20465639; DOI: 10.1111/j.1365-4632.2009.04209.x) enrolled "47 patients with IGH" ("A clinical survey was carried out on 47 patients with IGH.") and examined "four cases" ("We also studied the ultrastructure of four cases.") by electron microscopy, reporting: "The IGH lesions demonstrated decreased melanin pigment and reduced numbers of melanocytes by NKI/beteb and MART-1. The ultrastructural evaluation showed degenerative melanocytes and decreased melanosomes. One specimen had normal melanocytes with decreased melanosomes." Earlier histochemical and microscopic analyses similarly reported: "Light and electron-microscopic and histochemical studies showed only reduced numbers of hypoactive melanocytes. In no case were melanocytes completely absent, excluding vitiligo." (Wilson et al., 1982; PMID: 6183861; DOI: 10.2340/0001555562301306). A subsequent biopsy letter also documented melanocyte loss alongside senescence under the title "Melanocytes in idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis disappear and are senescent" (Kim, T. H. et al., 2022; PMID: 36394380; DOI: 10.1111/jdv.18757). Cultured melanocytes isolated from IGH lesions display enlarged cell bodies and shortened processes: in a study enrolling "six IGH patients and six controls" ("For this study, six IGH patients and six controls were enrolled."), Rani et al. (2018; PMID: 29516488; DOI: 10.1111/ijd.13960) observed: "Melanocytes from IGH patients were bigger in size with very small and retracted dendrites as compared to the control melanocytes."
⚬ Cellular senescence in epidermal melanocytes and dermal cells: Senescence markers are elevated in lesional IGH skin compared with controls or perilesional skin. Rani et al. (2018; PMID: 29516488; DOI: 10.1111/ijd.13960) reported: "Our results showed that expression of p16, p21, and hp1 was significantly higher in lesional skin of IGH patient as compared to healthy controls." In dermal compartments, Kim, J. Y. et al. (2020; PMID: 31823346; DOI: 10.1111/bjd.18801) observed: "In our study, the number of p16-positive cells was more significantly increased, especially in the dermis of lesional skin from patients with IGH compared with perilesional normal skin. Furthermore, p16-positive cells were presumed to be fibroblasts based on the shape and distribution of cells."
⚬ Melanosome transfer and distribution abnormalities: Two ultrastructural and cellular studies independently identify impaired melanosome transfer or uptake between melanocytes and keratinocytes, although structural findings vary across cohorts. Kakepis et al. (2014; PMID: 25088925; DOI: 10.1111/jdv.12646) reported on electron microscopy of IGH biopsies: "In the epidermis, melanocytes and melanosomes were normal in structure. In some areas, there was a reduced uptake of melanosomes by the keratinocytes." Conversely, Rani et al. (2018; PMID: 29516488; DOI: 10.1111/ijd.13960) found intracellular retention of pigment: "Melanin accumulation was more in the IGH patients as compared to the controls." In a broader mechanistic investigation of melanocyte senescence relevant to photoaged hypopigmentation (not restricted to IGH lesions), Park et al. (2023; PMID: 37554281; DOI: 10.7150/thno.84912) reported: "These results demonstrate that senescent melanocytes are characterized by glycolytic metabolism changes and a defective melanosome transport process, which may be related to impaired mitochondrial function, highlighting the importance of metabolic reprogramming in regulating melanocyte senescence."
⚬ Epidermal, keratinocyte, and dermal architectural changes: Classic histological features are variable rather than universal. Among "47 patients with IGH", Kim, S. K. et al. (2010; PMID: 20465639; DOI: 10.1111/j.1365-4632.2009.04209.x) found: "Histologically, we found hyperkeratosis in 18 cases (38.3%), but epidermal atrophy was present in only five cases (10.6%), and flattened rete ridges in seven cases (14.9%) compared to the normal skin." In that same cohort, early-onset lesions were noted: "About 30% of the patients had their initial lesions prior to 20 years of age. The arm was the most commonly affected site (53%)." In a cross-sectional biopsy study taking "biopsy specimens of hypochromic lesions and adjacent normal skin from 20 patients with IGH", Arbache et al. (2022; PMID: 35114009; DOI: 10.1111/ijd.16076) reported: "We found superficial dermal fibrosis in 90% (18/20) of our IGH cases and unreported keratinocyte cytoplasmic changes on electron microscopy." In contrast, Kakepis et al. (2014; PMID: 25088925; DOI: 10.1111/jdv.12646) observed: "In the dermis, fibroblasts were structurally normal. Also, most elastic and collagen fibres were normal, but there were focal elastotic changes."

Hypotheses and Unverified Areas in IGH

⚬ Paracrine senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) signaling from dermal fibroblasts: Direct in vivo identification of specific fibroblast-derived cytokines causing IGH in human lesions was not found. However, Kim, J. Y. et al. (2020; PMID: 31823346; DOI: 10.1111/bjd.18801) modeled fibroblast senescence in vitro—exposing "Primary human dermal fibroblasts (PHDFs)" to "three consecutive days of UVB" and transferring media "On the 15th day of culture of PHDFs" onto melanocytes "for 3 days"—and reported: "The UVB-senescent FB media did not affect the melanogenesis but induced melanocyte apoptosis and senescence." From these combined biopsy and in vitro data, the authors hypothesized: "our data suggest that senescent fibroblasts, which are increased in number in IGH lesions, might contribute to hypopigmentation in IGH by inducing the senescence and apoptosis of melanocytes by secreting SASP factors."
⚬ Intracellular melanin accumulation driving melanocyte senescence: Rani et al. (2018; PMID: 29516488; DOI: 10.1111/ijd.13960) proposed a causal direction that remains unproven in longitudinal human studies: "Accumulation of more melanin in the IGH melanocytes might be due to problem in the transfer of melanin from melanocytes to keratinocytes. Accumulation of melanin can lead to the senescence in the melanocytes of IGH patients."
⚬ Keratinocyte paracrine and phagocytic dysfunction: Although reduced melanosome uptake by keratinocytes (Kakepis et al., 2014; PMID: 25088925; DOI: 10.1111/jdv.12646) and keratinocyte cytoplasmic alterations (Arbache et al., 2022; PMID: 35114009; DOI: 10.1111/ijd.16076) have been observed ultrastructurally, specific altered keratinocyte signaling pathways (such as stem cell factor, endothelin-1, or PAR-2) measured directly inside human IGH lesions were not found in the retrieved primary IGH studies.
⚬ Somatic mutations in IGH: Wilson et al. (1982; PMID: 6183861; DOI: 10.2340/0001555562301306) proposed an enduring hypothesis based on histology: "The evidence indicates an age-related somatic mutation of melanocytes." Direct whole-exome, whole-genome, or targeted somatic mutation sequencing of microdissected IGH melanocytes confirming recurrent clonal driver mutations was not found.
⚬ Melanocyte stem cell (McSC) reservoirs in IGH: Direct quantification or lineage tracing of follicular or interfollicular melanocyte stem cell reservoirs specifically within human IGH lesions was not found. In murine hair-follicle biology (about hair greying and homeostatic McSC maintenance in mice, not IGH), Sun et al. (2023; PMID: 37076619; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-05960-6) reported that McSCs maintain themselves via reversible dedifferentiation between niche compartments: "These results identify a new model whereby dedifferentiation is integral to homeostatic stem cell maintenance and suggest that modulating McSC mobility may represent a new approach for the prevention of hair greying." Whether a parallel stem-cell niche mobility failure or follicular McSC depletion occurs in IGH remains unestablished.

2. Cell Therapy for Depigmented Skin

Nearly all clinical cell-therapy data for depigmented skin come from vitiligo and selected congenital or post-inflammatory leukodermas; dedicated modern clinical trials of cellular transplantation for IGH were not found.

A. Autologous Non-Cultured Melanocyte-Keratinocyte Transplantation Procedure (MKTP)

⚬ Conditions treated: Primarily stable segmental and non-segmental vitiligo (Zhang et al., 2021; DOI: 10.18632/aging.202472; Mulekar, 2005; PMID: 16207186; DOI: 10.1111/j.1365-4632.2005.02226.x; Abdul Latheef et al., 2023; DOI: 10.4103/pigmentinternational.pigmentinternational_54_21), plus smaller cohorts of nevus depigmentosus and piebaldism (Nuntawisuttiwong et al., 2024; PMID: 39507768; DOI: 10.2147/ccid.s485421). Note that an older tissue-grafting study (suction/cryo blister-roof autologous melanocyte grafting rather than enzymatic cell suspension MKTP) did include IGH alongside vitiligo and post-inflammatory leukoderma: "Patients with three types of leukoderma--vitiligo, idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis, and postinflammatory leukoderma--had successful repigmentation after transplantation of autologous melanocytes" with "Repigmentation was visible within 7 to 14 days." (Suvanprakorn et al., 1985; PMID: 3908515; DOI: 10.1016/s0190-9622(85)70247-2).
⚬ Longest follow-up:
  ⚬ In vitiligo, up to 9 years ("followed up for a period of 1-9 years" and "12-108 months;mean:43 months; median:36 months") in a retrospective series of "2283 cases of vitiligo" where "2171 patients (94. 4%) were followed up for at least 2 years" (Zhang et al., 2021; DOI: 10.18632/aging.202472).
  ⚬ In vitiligo, nevus depigmentosus, and piebaldism, up to 84 months (7 years) in a cohort of "23 patients (24 treated lesions)" in which "78.3% had segmental vitiligo, while the others had nevus depigmentosus, nonsegmental vitiligo, or piebaldism" (Nuntawisuttiwong et al., 2024; PMID: 39507768; DOI: 10.2147/ccid.s485421).
  ⚬ In vitiligo vulgaris, up to 6 years ("observed for a period up to 6 years") in "One hundred and forty-two patients with vitiligo vulgaris" using a donor shave biopsy "up to 1/10th the size of recipient area" (Mulekar, 2005; PMID: 16207186; DOI: 10.1111/j.1365-4632.2005.02226.x).
  ⚬ In childhood stable localized vitiligo, 4 years ("followed for a period of 4 years") across "20 cases of stable localized childhood vitiligo (10 segmental and 10 focal)" (Abdul Latheef et al., 2023; DOI: 10.4103/pigmentinternational.pigmentinternational_54_21).
⚬ Durability:
  ⚬ In vitiligo (2,283 patients): "excellent re-pigmentation was achieved in more than half of the lesions and the pigment retained at the end of the respective follow-up period", and "More than half of patients could attain additional re-pigmentation even 9 months after surgery. Only a few patients were noted partially to completely reduced pigmentation." (Zhang et al., 2021; DOI: 10.18632/aging.202472).
  ⚬ In vitiligo vulgaris (142 patients, up to 6 years): "Eighty (56%) patients showed excellent, 15 (11%) showed good, 13 (9%) showed fair and 34 (24%) showed poor repigmentation, which was retained till the end of the respective follow-up period." (Mulekar, 2005; PMID: 16207186; DOI: 10.1111/j.1365-4632.2005.02226.x).
  ⚬ In vitiligo and other leukodermas (23 patients, up to 84 months): "At the 12-month follow-up, repigmentation showed an 80.8% ± 19.3% VASI improvement, which was sustained over 84 months with an 80%-90% VASI improvement." Specifically for non-vitiligo cases: "For nevus depigmentosus, 3 patients showed an average improvement of 80.0% ± 8.7% at the 1-year follow-up, maintaining 80–90% repigmentation over 36 months. One case of piebaldism exhibited a 90% improvement in VASI at the 1-year follow-up." (Nuntawisuttiwong et al., 2024; PMID: 39507768; DOI: 10.2147/ccid.s485421).
  ⚬ In childhood vitiligo (20 patients, 4 years): "Out of total 20 cases, 11 had excellent (90–100%) response, 4 had good (60–89%), 2 had fair (25–59%), and 3 had poor response (0–24%)." (Abdul Latheef et al., 2023; DOI: 10.4103/pigmentinternational.pigmentinternational_54_21).
⚬ Regulatory status: Conventional non-cultured MKTP is performed as a same-day autologous surgical procedure (Mulekar, 2005; PMID: 16207186; DOI: 10.1111/j.1365-4632.2005.02226.x; Nuntawisuttiwong et al., 2024; PMID: 39507768; DOI: 10.2147/ccid.s485421). A formal regulatory drug/biologic approval dossier for manual non-cultured MKTP was not found in the retrieved PMID/DOI/ClinicalTrials.gov records.

B. Commercial Point-of-Care Autologous Skin Cell Suspension (ASCS / RECELL)

⚬ Conditions treated: Stable vitiligo ("Focal, segmental or generalized (i.e., nonsegmental) stable vitiligo, defined as no new depigmented areas nor any depigmented areas that have expanded in size within the preceding 12 months", lesions "between 16cm2 and 456cm2 (contiguous)" and "judged clinically as ≥90% depigmented (by area)" in adults "18 years of age or older"; NCT04547998). Earlier pilot evaluation was also conducted in vitiligo (Mulekar et al., 2007; PMID: 17927795; DOI: 10.1111/j.1365-2133.2007.08216.x). Use in IGH was not found.
⚬ Longest follow-up: In the pivotal within-subject randomized controlled trial (NCT04547998), primary repigmentation assessment occurred at "Week 24" with total study participation of "52 weeks" ("duration of his/her participation in the study (52 weeks)"). In the early comparative pilot study by Mulekar et al. (2007; PMID: 17927795; DOI: 10.1111/j.1365-2133.2007.08216.x), "Ten lesions in five patients" were evaluated "at 4 months post-transplantation." Multi-year follow-up studies specific to RECELL in vitiligo were not found in the retrieved PMID/DOI/ClinicalTrials.gov records.
⚬ Durability: In the 4-month pilot study in vitiligo, "Of the five lesions treated with ReCell two lesions showed 100%, one 65% and one 40% repigmentation, and one lesion failed to repigment. Of the five lesions treated by conventional MKT three showed 100% and one 30% repigmentation and one failed to repigment." (Mulekar et al., 2007; PMID: 17927795; DOI: 10.1111/j.1365-2133.2007.08216.x). Multi-year durability outcomes from NCT04547998 were not found in the retrieved trial record snippet.
⚬ Regulatory status: NCT04547998 was sponsored by Avita Medical as a pivotal clinical study of the RECELL device ("Spray-On Skin™ Cells prepared using RECELL will be applied to an area prepared by ablative laser, followed by targeted narrowband UVB phototherapy"). Exact FDA marketing-authorization date and PMA identifier with a corresponding PMID/DOI/ClinicalTrials.gov ID were not found in the qualifying retrieved records (see Methods/Scope note on regulatory databases).

C. Cultured Autologous Melanocyte Transplantation

⚬ Conditions treated: Stable segmental and non-segmental vitiligo (Lin et al., 2024; PMID: 38895831; DOI: 10.1111/1346-8138.17320). Trials of cultured melanocyte transplantation in IGH were not found.
⚬ Longest follow-up: Up to 12 years ("All patients were followed up for at least 3 months, with a maximum of 12 years") in a retrospective study of "491 patients with long‐term follow‐up data (12–120 months, mean 43 months, median 36 months)" whose "duration of vitiligo ranged from 1 to 30 years, with a mean duration of 6.5 years" (Lin et al., 2024; PMID: 38895831; DOI: 10.1111/1346-8138.17320).
⚬ Durability: In vitiligo (491 patients), Lin et al. (2024; PMID: 38895831; DOI: 10.1111/1346-8138.17320) reported: "In total, 123 (5.4%) patients experienced vitiligo recurrence after 12 years." Among lesions stable for 1 year: "Among the 201 lesions with stable vitiligo for 1 year, 99 lesions had >90% repigmentation, accounting for 49.2%, and 164 lesions of the 201 lesions had >50% repigmentation, accounting for 81.5%. The average degree of pigmentation was 69.5%."
⚬ Regulatory status: Conducted clinically at specialized academic hospital centers (e.g., Hangzhou Third People's Hospital in China; Lin et al., 2024; PMID: 38895831; DOI: 10.1111/1346-8138.17320). FDA or EMA marketing approval for a commercial cultured melanocyte product was not found.

D. Stem-Cell-Derived Melanocytes (iPSC- or MSC-Derived)

⚬ Conditions treated: Strictly preclinical modeling aimed at vitiligo and tissue-engineered skin; human clinical trials in any pigmentary disorder (vitiligo or IGH) were not found. Xie et al. (2022; DOI: 10.1016/j.reth.2022.06.007) induced mouse bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells into melanocyte-like cells ("we have induced mouse bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMMSCs) into melanocytes (miMels)") and transplanted tissue-engineered skin onto nude mice ("we tried to transplant tissue-engineered skin on the back skin of nude mice and succeeded. The transplanted miMels survived in local tissues, synthesized active tyrosinase and melanin, and expressed the marker protein of melanocytes."). Protocols for differentiating human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) into epidermal cells for vitiligo remain methodological/preclinical (Arjmand et al., 2024; PMID: 38189899; DOI: 10.1007/7651_2023_510).
⚬ Longest follow-up: Human clinical follow-up not found (preclinical murine models only; Xie et al., 2022; DOI: 10.1016/j.reth.2022.06.007).
⚬ Durability: Human clinical durability not found.
⚬ Regulatory status: Investigational/preclinical only; no approved product or registered clinical trial was found.

> **Not checked.** Sections 3, 4 and 5 below, the reference list and the summary table were not verified against any source. Treat every name, number, trial ID and quote in them as an unconfirmed lead.

3. Gene Therapy, Gene Editing, and RNA Delivery in Skin (Any Condition)

All approved products and late-stage clinical programs for skin gene therapy, gene editing, and RNA delivery target inherited blistering disorders (epidermolysis bullosa), genodermatoses, cutaneous neoplasms, wound healing, or autoimmune inflammation—none target IGH.

A. Approved and Pivotal/Late-Stage Gene Therapies in Skin

⚬ Beremagene geperpavec (B-VEC / Vyjuvek) — Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa (DEB) (not IGH):
  ⚬ Regulatory status: FDA-approved topical gene therapy: "Vyjuvek, a Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved medication" and "Vyjuvek is the first topical gene therapy for DEB, utilizing a genetically modified HSV-1 (herpes simplex virus 1) vector to express human COL7 and promote wound healing" for a disorder "with an estimated prevalence of two to six cases per million live births" (Khan et al., 2023; PMID: 38098548; DOI: 10.1097/ms9.0000000000001422).
  ⚬ Pivotal trial evidence (NCT04491604 / GEM-3): In a Phase 3 intra-patient randomized trial, "Primary wound pairs were exposed to B-VEC and placebo in 31 patients. At 6 months, complete wound healing occurred in 67% of the wounds exposed to B-VEC as compared with 22% of those exposed to placebo" (Guide et al., 2022; PMID: 36516090; DOI: 10.1056/nejmoa2206663).
  ⚬ Delivery method: Topical gel containing a replication-defective herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) vector applied directly to open skin wounds (episomal, non-integrating; requires repeat application) (Khan et al., 2023; PMID: 38098548; DOI: 10.1097/ms9.0000000000001422).
  ⚬ Single known gene fault required? Yes. B-VEC replaces a single defective gene (COL7A1), restoring type VII collagen ("Mutations in the COL7A1 (collagen type VII alpha 1 gene) gene, which encodes COL7, result in weakened anchoring fibrils"; Khan et al., 2023; PMID: 38098548; DOI: 10.1097/ms9.0000000000001422).
⚬ EB-101 / Prademagene zamikeracel (pz-cel) — Recessive Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa (RDEB) (not IGH):
  ⚬ Late-stage trials and status: Evaluated in Phase 1/2a (NCT01263379) with "long-term (mean 5.9 years, range 4–8 years) efficacy and safety data on seven adults treated with EB-101 for severe RDEB wounds" (So et al., 2022; PMID: 36253825; DOI: 10.1186/s13023-022-02546-9), followed by the Phase 3 VIITAL trial (NCT04227106: "Phase 3, Open-label Clinical Trial of EB-101 for the Treatment of Recessive Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa (RDEB)") and a Phase 4 master protocol (NCT07717736: "Study C assesses the efficacy and safety of pz-cel in patient populations not represented in the VIITAL clinical trial (NCT04227106)").
  ⚬ Delivery method: Ex vivo retroviral gene correction of autologous keratinocytes grown into epidermal cellular sheets and surgically grafted onto chronic wounds (So et al., 2022; PMID: 36253825; DOI: 10.1186/s13023-022-02546-9).
  ⚬ Single known gene fault required? Yes (COL7A1).
⚬ FCX-007 (Dabocemagene autoficel) — RDEB (not IGH):
  ⚬ Late-stage trial: Phase 3 DEFI-RDEB (NCT04213261), enrolling "approximately 24 subjects" aged "≥2 years of age" with "Up to three target wound pairs" per subject and "confirmation of COL7A1 genetic mutation".
  ⚬ Delivery method: Intradermal/local injection of ex vivo genetically corrected autologous dermal fibroblasts ("FCX-007 is comprised of fibroblasts isolated from the subject's skin biopsies which are genetically corrected with the full length COL7A1 gene encoding for type VII collagen"; NCT04213261).
  ⚬ Single known gene fault required? Yes (COL7A1).
⚬ Ex Vivo Epidermal Stem Cell Gene Therapy — Junctional Epidermolysis Bullosa (JEB) & RDEB (not IGH):
  ⚬ Clinical landmark and pivotal trial: In a foundational single-patient compassionate-use study of JEB, Hirsch et al. (2017; PMID: 29144448; DOI: 10.1038/nature24487) achieved "life-saving regeneration of virtually the entire epidermis (~0.85 m2) on a 7-year-old child suffering from a devastating form of JEB by means of autologous transgenic keratinocyte cultures" who had "epidermal loss on ~80% of his body", showing "The regenerated epidermis remained robust, resistant to mechanical stress and did not develop blisters or erosions during 21 months follow-up", sustained by self-renewing epidermal stem cells (holoclones). A subsequent Phase II/III pivotal trial (NCT05111600, Hologene 5, patients "between 6 months and 65 years old", "Approximately 2 months" GMP production, "12 months" follow-up, primary endpoint "Re-epithelialization in absence of blisters in at least 50% of the transplanted area") evaluated autologous genetically modified epidermal stem cell grafts for JEB. In RDEB, the Phase I/II EBGraft trial (NCT04186650) evaluates "3 adult subjects" (aged "18 years", wounds "≥100cm2", grafted areas "up to 300 cm2", biopsied through "Month 12 post grafting") using a "COL7A1-SIN retroviral vector engineered autologous tissue-engineered skin" ("confirmed bi-allelic COL7A1 mutations").
  ⚬ Single known gene fault required? Yes (LAMB3 in Hirsch et al., 2017; PMID: 29144448; DOI: 10.1038/nature24487; COL7A1 in NCT04186650).
⚬ KB105 — Topical HSV-1 Gene Therapy for Autosomal Recessive Congenital Ichthyosis (not IGH):
  ⚬ Trial and delivery: Phase I/II (NCT04047732) evaluating "Topical, Replication-defective" HSV-1 gene therapy (KB105) sponsored by Krystal Biotech (Søgaard et al., 2021; DOI: 10.3390/pharmaceutics13101722; Ain et al., 2021; DOI: 10.1016/j.tibtech.2020.07.012).
  ⚬ Single known gene fault required? Yes (monogenic replacement).

B. Gene Editing (CRISPR-Cas9 / Base Editing) in Skin

⚬ Approved products / late-stage clinical trials: Not found. No approved skin gene-editing therapy and no active human clinical trials of in vivo or ex vivo CRISPR gene editing for skin diseases were found in the retrieved PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov records.
⚬ Current state and delivery method: Preclinical ex vivo editing of patient-derived keratinocytes or iPSCs for monogenic genodermatoses such as epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS) and RDEB (not IGH). Sheriff & Jacków-Malinowska (2024; DOI: 10.1016/j.ymthe.2024.01.017) summarize that investigators "deploy an allele-specific gene-editing strategy using clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-associated nuclease-Cas9 (CRISPR-Cas9) to reverse the pathogenicity of EBS in patient-derived keratinocytes", shifting "from lentiviral integration to RNP complexes delivered by electroporation", while noting that in situ skin delivery via lipid nanoparticles ("RNP complexes... could feasibly be encapsulated by lipid nanoparticles for in situ editing, a method recently shown to be effective on excised human skin") remains preclinical. Reviews of vitiligo drug delivery likewise cite CRISPR-Cas9 only as a conceptual future direction (Sahu et al., 2025; PMID: 39716607; DOI: 10.1016/j.ijpharm.2024.125106).
⚬ Single known gene fault required? Usually yes for sequence correction (e.g., allele-specific knockout of dominant-negative keratin mutations or homology-directed repair of recessive mutations; Sheriff & Jacków-Malinowska, 2024; DOI: 10.1016/j.ymthe.2024.01.017). Technically, CRISPR/epigenetic editing can also silence or activate non-mutated regulatory genes, but clinical validation of that approach in skin was not found.

C. RNA Delivery in Skin (siRNA, mRNA, Antisense Oligonucleotides)

⚬ Approved products for skin: Not found.
⚬ Clinical and late-preclinical trials:
  ⚬ Dual siRNA (STP705) — Basal Cell Carcinoma (not IGH): Phase 2 open-label dose-escalation trial (NCT04669808, Sirnaomics) evaluating localized "intra-and peri-lesional injection" of STP705 targeting "TGF-β1 and COX-2" across "35 patients" divided "equally among 7 cohorts (30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, and 320 μg dose level) of 5 patients each", administered "once a week for 6 weeks".
  ⚬ Modified mRNA (AZD8601 encoding VEGF-A165) — Type 2 Diabetes Forearm Skin / Wound Angiogenesis (not IGH): Phase 1 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT02935712, AstraZeneca; planned "up to 60 male patients with T2DM aged 18 to 65 years", enrolled men "aged 41–65"), delivering chemically modified mRNA "formulated in citrate-buffered saline and given by intradermal injection into the forearm skin", with "microdialysis for 28 h after administration". Gan et al. (2019; PMID: 30787295; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-019-08852-4) concluded: "Intradermal VEGF-A mRNA was well tolerated and led to local functional VEGF-A protein expression and transient skin blood flow enhancement in men with T2DM."
  ⚬ Antisense Oligonucleotide (QR-313) — RDEB (not IGH): First-in-human Phase I/II trial (NCT03605069) of topical/local antisense oligonucleotide designed for exon skipping ("QR-313 hybridizes to a specific sequence in the COL7A1 pre-mRNA to exclude" the mutated exon; Søgaard et al., 2021; DOI: 10.3390/pharmaceutics13101722; Ain et al., 2021; DOI: 10.1016/j.tibtech.2020.07.012).
  ⚬ JAK1-selective siRNA — Vitiligo (preclinical murine model, not IGH): Tang et al. (2023; PMID: 37925520; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-42714-4) designed a chemically stabilized JAK1-selective siRNA tested via local skin administration in a mouse model of autoimmune vitiligo ("In a mouse model of vitiligo, local administration of the JAK1 siRNA" modulated skin autoimmunity). Human trial data for this candidate were not found.
⚬ Single known gene fault required?
  ⚬ Antisense exon-skipping (QR-313): Yes—targets a specific mutation-bearing exon in COL7A1 (Søgaard et al., 2021; DOI: 10.3390/pharmaceutics13101722).
  ⚬ siRNA and mRNA (STP705, AZD8601, JAK1 siRNA): No. Neither requires a single monogenic mutation; siRNA transiently silences an overactive wild-type pathway (e.g., TGF-β1/COX-2 in NCT04669808; JAK1 in Tang et al., 2023; PMID: 37925520; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-42714-4), and mRNA transiently expresses a wild-type paracrine protein (e.g., VEGF-A165 in Gan et al., 2019; PMID: 30787295; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-019-08852-4).

4. Applicability Assessment for IGH: Required Conditions vs. Existing Evidence

Modality (from Sections 2 & 3)	What Would Have to Be True About IGH for This Approach to Apply	Does Evidence for That Exist in IGH?
Non-cultured MKTP & Point-of-Care ASCS (RECELL)	(1) Repigmentation fails because local epidermal melanocytes are depleted or irreversibly senescent; (2) the IGH dermal/epidermal microenvironment can support survival and dendrite/melanosome transfer of freshly transplanted normal melanocytes and keratinocytes without immediately re-inducing senescence; (3) the risk-benefit of epidermal ablation plus grafting justifies treating small, scattered benign macules.	Partial / Mixed. Melanocyte reduction and senescence are established (Kim, S. K. et al., 2010; PMID: 20465639; Rani et al., 2018; PMID: 29516488; Kim, T. H. et al., 2022; PMID: 36394380), and one 1985 blister-roof grafting study reported repigmentation in IGH (Suvanprakorn et al., 1985; PMID: 3908515). However, superficial dermal fibrosis in "90% (18/20)" of lesions (Arbache et al., 2022; PMID: 35114009) and dermal p16-positive senescent fibroblasts that induce melanocyte senescence/apoptosis in vitro (Kim, J. Y. et al., 2020; PMID: 31823346) raise the unresolved risk that the IGH dermis could impair long-term graft survival. Modern MKTP or ASCS trials in IGH were not found.
Cultured Autologous Melanocytes	Same biological prerequisites as MKTP, plus either (1) IGH requires expanding very small donor biopsies to cover large depigmented areas, or (2) pure melanocytes alone (without fresh donor keratinocytes) can overcome lesional keratinocyte transfer defects.	Weak / Unproven. Two IGH ultrastructural studies implicate keratinocyte melanosome uptake or cytoplasmic defects (Kakepis et al., 2014; PMID: 25088925; Arbache et al., 2022; PMID: 35114009). If lesional keratinocytes remain defective in phagocytosis, transplanting pure melanocytes alone may underperform compared with melanocyte-keratinocyte co-transplantation. Clinical data in IGH were not found.
Stem-Cell-Derived Melanocytes (iPSC / MSC)	Same biological prerequisites as cultured melanocytes, plus demonstration of human safety, absence of tumorigenicity, long-term survival, and functional melanosome transfer in human skin.	No. Human clinical evidence does not exist for any pigment disorder; only murine preclinical tissue-engineering data were found (Xie et al., 2022; DOI: 10.1016/j.reth.2022.06.007).
Gene Replacement Therapy (Viral HSV-1 or Ex Vivo Retroviral, e.g., B-VEC, EB-101, FCX-007)	Either (1) IGH is caused by a single recurrent loss-of-function gene defect in epidermal or dermal cells, or (2) sustained overexpression of a single therapeutic wild-type gene (e.g., a melanogenic or anti-senescence factor) is sufficient to reverse established IGH lesions without disrupting skin homeostasis; additionally, topical vectors like HSV-1 would need to cross intact stratum corneum (unlike open EB wounds).	No. No single causal monogenic or recurrent somatic driver mutation has been identified in IGH (only hypothesized by Wilson et al., 1982; PMID: 6183861). Furthermore, intact IGH epidermis lacks the chronic ulceration/blistering that allows topical B-VEC access in DEB (Khan et al., 2023; PMID: 38098548).
Gene Editing (CRISPR-Cas9 / Base Editing)	A defined, recurrent causal mutation or single validated genetic switch in IGH melanocytes, keratinocytes, or dermal fibroblasts whose permanent edit restores pigmentation safely across intact skin.	No. No validated causal somatic mutation or genetic target in IGH was found, and clinical human skin delivery of CRISPR remains preclinical even for single-gene diseases (Sheriff & Jacków-Malinowska, 2024; DOI: 10.1016/j.ymthe.2024.01.017).
RNA Delivery (siRNA / mRNA / ASO)	For ASO exon skipping: a defined single-gene mutation (absent in IGH). For siRNA or mRNA: a single-gene mutation is not required, but IGH lesions would need (1) viable resident melanocytes (or recruitable stem cells) that remain responsive to transient paracrine/metabolic modulation, and (2) an identified druggable pathway (e.g., a specific SASP cytokine, senescence regulator such as p16/p21, or melanosome-transport regulator) whose transient knockdown (siRNA) or protein expression (mRNA) produces durable repigmentation after intradermal or transdermal delivery.	Biological plausibility only; direct clinical evidence not found. Direct observations confirm that residual melanocytes are typically still present (Wilson et al., 1982; PMID: 6183861; Kim, S. K. et al., 2010; PMID: 20465639) and exhibit elevated p16/p21/hp1 expression and glycolytic/melanosome-transport dysfunction alongside dermal p16-positive cells (Rani et al., 2018; PMID: 29516488; Kim, J. Y. et al., 2020; PMID: 31823346; Park et al., 2023; PMID: 37554281). Proof-of-concept human intradermal mRNA translation (Gan et al., 2019; PMID: 30787295) and intralesional siRNA delivery (NCT04669808) exist for other skin conditions, but no RNA target has been clinically tested in IGH.

5. Active Research Groups and Trial Sponsors

IGH and Melanocyte Senescence / Aging Pigment Biology

K. et al., 2010; PMID: 20465639; Kim, T. H. et al., 2022; PMID: 36394380; Park et al., 2023; PMID: 37554281).
⚬ Sang Ho Oh Group (Yonsei University / collaborators, South Korea): Studying dermal p16-positive senescent fibroblasts and UVB-induced SASP effects on melanocyte apoptosis and senescence in IGH (Kim, J. Y. et al., 2020; PMID: 31823346).
⚬ Davinder Parsad Group (Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh, India): Investigating IGH melanocyte morphology, melanin retention, and senescence markers (p16, p21, hp1) (Rani et al., 2018; PMID: 29516488).
⚬ Samir Arbache & Sergio H. Hirata Group (Universidade Federal de São Paulo — UNIFESP, Brazil): Investigating dermal fibrosis and keratinocyte ultrastructure in IGH (Arbache et al., 2022; PMID: 35114009).
⚬ Mayumi Ito Group (NYU Langone Health, New York, USA): Studying follicular melanocyte stem cell (McSC) niche mobility and dedifferentiation in aging/hair greying (not IGH) (Sun et al., 2023; PMID: 37076619).

Cell Therapy for Depigmented Skin (Vitiligo and Non-IGH Leukodermas)

⚬ Avita Medical (Trial Sponsor, NCT04547998): Commercial sponsor of the RECELL autologous skin cell suspension system evaluated in stable vitiligo.
⚬ Ai-E Xu Group (Hangzhou Third People's Hospital Affiliated to Zhejiang Chinese Medical University, Hangzhou, China): Leading high-volume long-term follow-up cohorts for both non-cultured MKTP (2,283 patients; Zhang et al., 2021; DOI: 10.18632/aging.202472) and cultured pure melanocyte transplantation (491 patients; Lin et al., 2024; PMID: 38895831).
⚬ Narumol Silpa-Archa Group (Siriraj MKTP Clinic, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand): Long-term MKTP outcomes in vitiligo, nevus depigmentosus, and piebaldism (Nuntawisuttiwong et al., 2024; PMID: 39507768).
⚬ Sanjeev V. Mulekar & Collaborators (Saudi Arabia / India): Foundational long-term MKTP and early RECELL pilot studies in vitiligo (Mulekar, 2005; PMID: 16207186; Mulekar et al., 2007; PMID: 17927795).
⚬ Xingyu Mei / Weimin Shi Group (China) and Babak Arjmand Group (Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Iran): Preclinical MSC-derived and iPSC-derived epidermal/pigment cell approaches for vitiligo (Xie et al., 2022; DOI: 10.1016/j.reth.2022.06.007; Arjmand et al., 2024; PMID: 38189899).

## Quote check (sections 1 and 2 only), 2026-11-28

Checked by a cloud thread against saved source text, using the verifier standard in `.claude/agents/verifier.md`: a quote passes only if the exact words appear in the saved source. Sources were fetched on 2026-11-28 from PubMed E-utilities (abstracts), NCBI PMC (open-access full text), Crossref (one abstract absent from PubMed) and the ClinicalTrials.gov API, and saved to the project files folder under `papers/excerpts/`. Matching ignored line breaks only; any other difference is shown in the table.

**Result.** 63 quoted strings checked. 56 found word for word (44 in an abstract or registry record, 12 only in open-access full text). 7 not in any text we can read, all from one paper (Kim JY 2020, PMID 31823346). 0 altered quotes. 0 mismatched identifiers: every PMID's PubMed title matches the paper described, and the three DOI-only citations resolve correctly (Zhang 2021 = PMID 33582653, Xie 2022 = PMID 35844295, Abdul Latheef 2023 = Crossref record, not in PubMed).

### Points Ben should not rely on

1. **The senescent fibroblast mechanism (Kim JY 2020, PMID 31823346).** All seven quotes from it are unreadable here: PubMed carries no abstract, NCBI's ID converter says it is not in PMC, and Europe PMC returned HTTP 503 on 2026-11-28. The words may well be in the letter, but until the PDF is read they are a lead. Section 4 of the report leans on this paper for its "the IGH dermis could impair graft survival" point.
2. **"Melanocytes disappear and are senescent" (Kim TH 2022, PMID 36394380).** Only the title exists in PubMed, so what was measured and in how many people is unknown. Already on the project paywall list as kim2023.
3. **Lin 2024 durability figures (PMID 38895831).** The paper disagrees with itself: its abstract says follow-up 6 to 120 months, its results say 12 to 120 months and separately "a maximum of 12 years" for patients treated 2009 to 2020. And "123 (5.4%) patients experienced vitiligo recurrence" cannot be a share of 491 patients, which would be 25.1 per cent; the same "123 ... (5. 4%)" appears in Zhang 2021 from the same hospital as a Koebner-phenomenon count out of 2283. Gemini copied the sentences faithfully, so the fault is in the paper, but "up to 12 years" and "5.4% recurrence" should not be used.
4. **"Durability" in section 2 is partial repigmentation, not a colour match.** Every durability quote is a VASI score or a graded repigmentation category. Under rule 4 of `CLAUDE.md` those are partial repigmentation, not lasting colour match. None of these papers reports a measured colour match against surrounding skin, and whether any patient had a second procedure was not checked.
5. **Smaller wording points.** Rani 2018 says cultured melanocytes "from the IGH patients", not from lesions. Nuntawisuttiwong 2024 followed patients 12 to 84 months, so "sustained over 84 months" describes the longest-followed patients, not the cohort. The report's summary table says sample size "not found" for Wilson 1982 (the abstract says 20 cases), Kakepis 2014 (four patients) and NCT04547998 (the registry shows 25 enrolled, results posted 2023-09-21, with a Week 24 outcome named "Color Matching").

### New to the project (Gate A candidates)

None for Module 1. All eight IGH papers cited in sections 1 and 2 are already in `data/search_log.csv` and `data/screening_log.csv`: PMID 3908515 (suvanprakorn1985, in the ledger); 20465639, 6183861 and 25088925 (screened, excluded from Module 1 as having no intervention); 29516488, 31823346, 35114009 and 36394380 (already listed as leads without a treatment arm).

Four non-IGH sources in sections 1 and 2 appear in no earlier search or screening log, so they are Module 5 leads only, for Ben to accept or drop at Gate A: PMID 17927795 (Mulekar 2007, ReCell pilot in vitiligo), PMID 38895831 (Lin 2024, cultured melanocytes in vitiligo, with the contradiction above), PMID 35844295 (Xie 2022, mouse MSC-derived melanocytes) and PMID 38189899 (Arjmand 2024, iPSC keratinocyte laboratory protocol). Abdul Latheef 2023 and NCT04547998 are also new to the logs. No extraction was done on any of them.
